questions.q: Which of these are jobs done by an operating system? Tick all that apply.
options: Writing the programs the user runs
questions.feedback: Five management jobs plus the interface. Compressing a file is a utility, and the operating system does not write anybody's programs.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 2: What the OS does

questions.q: State what is meant by systems software.

markPoints.concept: software that runs and manages the computer itself, rather than doing a job for the user
markPoints.exemplar: Software that runs and manages the computer itself.

questions.example: Software that runs and manages the computer itself, such as the operating system and utilities, rather than application software that does a job for the user.
questions.paraphrase: Programs that control and look after the machine rather than carrying out a task for the person using it.
questions.feedback: Managing the computer. Naming examples without saying what they do is half an answer.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 2: What the OS does

questions.q: Match each kind of user interface to a situation it suits.
pairs: A pupil using a laptop to write an essay
A technician writing a script to set up fifty machines at once
A cash machine with a few fixed choices
A driver who needs their hands on the wheel
questions.feedback: Each interface suits a different balance of ease and control.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 3: Graphical user interface

questions.q: Explain why a technician might prefer a command line interface to a graphical one.

markPoints.concept: commands can be combined into a script and run automatically
markPoints.exemplar: Commands can be written into a script and run automatically.

markPoints.concept: so a long or repeated job is done far faster than clicking through it
accept: faster|quicker|less time|saves time|far more|more efficient|without clicking|no clicking|one go
markPoints.exemplar: This means a repeated job is done far faster than clicking through a graphical interface.

questions.example: A command line lets commands be written into a script and run automatically, so a job that has to be repeated across fifty machines is done in one go rather than by clicking through the same windows fifty times.
questions.paraphrase: Typed commands can be saved into a script and executed without supervision, which means a repetitive task finishes far more quickly than working through menus would allow.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 3: Graphical user interface

questions.q: Explain one disadvantage of a command line interface for an ordinary user.

markPoints.concept: the user has to know the commands
markPoints.exemplar: The user has to know the exact commands.

markPoints.concept: so it is harder to learn and a mistyped command may do something unintended
markPoints.exemplar: This makes it much harder to learn than clicking on an icon.

questions.example: A command line gives no clues: the user has to know the exact command and type it correctly, so it is much harder to learn than pointing at an icon, and one mistyped command can do real damage.
questions.paraphrase: Nothing on the screen tells you what is available, so you must already know the commands and type them exactly, which makes it far harder to pick up than clicking on pictures.
questions.feedback: What the user must know, and what follows from not knowing it.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 3: Graphical user interface

questions.q: Sort each program by whether it is systems software or application software.
questions.feedback: Systems software looks after the computer. Application software does a job for the person using it.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 1: What is systems software?

questions.q: Which of these could a computer not start up without?
questions.feedback: Everything else runs on top of the operating system, which is why it is loaded first.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 1: What is systems software?

questions.q: Which of these are features of a graphical user interface? Tick all that apply.
options: Windows that can be moved and resized
Icons that stand for programs and files
Menus the user can read rather than remember
A pointer controlled by a mouse or a finger
A list of numbered choices and nothing else
correct: Windows that can be moved and resized
Icons that stand for programs and files
Menus the user can read rather than remember
A pointer controlled by a mouse or a finger
questions.feedback: Windows, icons, menus and a pointer. Typed commands belong to a command line, and a numbered list to a menu driven interface.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 3: Graphical user interface

questions.q: Explain why a graphical user interface needs more memory and processing power than a command line interface.

markPoints.concept: the graphics themselves have to be drawn and kept in memory
markPoints.exemplar: The windows, icons and pointer all have to be drawn and held in memory.

markPoints.concept: so there is far more for the computer to keep track of than lines of text
markPoints.exemplar: This means there is far more to keep track of than the lines of text a command line needs.

questions.example: A graphical interface has to draw windows, icons and a moving pointer, and keep all of it in memory so it can be redrawn whenever anything moves. A command line only has to hold and display lines of text, so there is far more for the computer to keep track of.
questions.paraphrase: Because the pictures, windows and pointer must all be produced and stored, the machine has much more to handle than it would for plain typed text.
questions.feedback: What has to be drawn and stored, and how that compares with text.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 3: Graphical user interface

questions.q: A cash machine offers five choices on screen and nothing else. What kind of interface is this?
questions.feedback: A fixed set of choices and no free movement is what makes it menu driven. It also means the user cannot reach anything they should not.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 5: Menu driven and voice

questions.q: Explain one advantage of a menu driven interface for a machine used by the public.

markPoints.concept: the user can only choose from the options offered
markPoints.exemplar: The user can only choose from the options on the menu.

markPoints.concept: so nothing has to be learned and nothing can be broken
accept: no training|without training|without being taught|nothing to learn|no need to know|easy|simple|anyone|anybody|cannot break|cannot damage|cannot reach|cannot wander|cannot get into|safe|secure|mistake
markPoints.exemplar: This means anybody can use it without training, and they cannot reach anything they should not.

questions.example: A menu driven interface offers a fixed set of choices and nothing else, so a member of the public can use it without being taught anything, and cannot wander into settings or files that are none of their business.
questions.paraphrase: Since only the listed options are available, no training is required and the user has no way of reaching parts of the system they should not touch.
questions.feedback: Limited choices, and the two things that limit buys you.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 5: Menu driven and voice

questions.q: A voice interface is a good choice for a user whose hands are busy.
questions.feedback: That is the situation it is for: driving, cooking, or working with tools.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.5 Lesson 1 — Control room, station 5: Menu driven and voice
